column2: Airport baggage X-ray. The glass is the screener's monitor: a carry-on bag sits in the tunnel, seen in the classic false colour (orange organics, green mixed, blue metal, black dense, on a white field), with the scanner's scrolling acquisition, a hunting zoom loupe and the operator's crosshair always moving at 60 fps. The time is made of the things packed inside the bag: keys, scissors, a coiled charger cable, a hair dryer, a banana, a rubber duck, a camera, a slinky... arranged so each digit is a cluster of overlapping objects (a 0 a coiled belt, a 1 an umbrella, an 8 a pair of sunglasses over headphones), translucent and overlapping as X-rays really are. Design all ten digit-packings as a set. Minute turn: the belt moves, the old bag slides out of the tunnel and the next bag scrolls in line by line under the scan bar (old digit gone before :00, new one after). Hour: a bigger show, e.g. a 'bag check' alarm with a red threat box, the tunnel's view switching mode (organic-only, inverted, edge-enhanced) and back. 2:1 suits the tunnel strip. Keep the false-colour palette honest.

Synchronised swimming, top-down, Busby Berkeley style. The glass is a pool seen from the high diving board: turquoise water with real moving caustics over tiled floor and lane lines, sunlight glints, ripples. The time is formed by the swimmers themselves: dozens of swimmers in matching caps and suits floating on their backs, holding hands or legs, whose formation makes each digit (a kaleidoscopic Berkeley flower that resolves into numerals), sculling, kicking, rotating, always alive. Design the ten formations as a set. Minute turn: the changing digit's swimmers dive under (only bubbles and rings show), swim underwater and surface in the new formation, choreographed, eased, every swimmer on a smooth path. Hour: the big number, e.g. the whole team blooms into a kaleidoscope wheel that spins and opens into the new time, or a team of divers drops in. Swimmers must read as people from above at --scale 4 (bold caps, arms, splashes). A coach or lifeguard on deck is welcome.

The circuit board. The glass shows a macro view of a green PCB (soldermask, gold pads, white silkscreen, vias, SMD parts, a QFN chip), and the numerals ARE copper traces: 45-degree routing, rounded corners, pads at the stroke ends, vias at joints, neck-downs, ground pours with thermal reliefs: a typeface designed as a set by a PCB layout engineer. Current flows: bright pulses travel along the traces at 60 fps, tiny LEDs blink, a crystal ticks the seconds. Minute turn: the old digit's traces are etched away (copper dissolving to bare fibreglass) and the autorouter lays the new digit's traces live, segment by segment, followed by a solder wave or reflow shimmer; the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the board powers up: a boot sequence lights everything, a scope probe touches down, or the whole board flips to a fresh layer (top/bottom copper in different mask colours). Silkscreen labels (in silkscreen-style type) are welcome as secondary detail, but the clock is the hero.

The moon rabbits make mochi. On a silver-grey lunar landscape (craters, regolith, the blue Earth hanging in the black sky, stars), two or three bold white rabbits with a big wooden mallet (kine) and a stone mortar (usu) pound and shape mochi, which is the material of the numerals: soft, puffy, flour-dusted, slightly glossy rice-cake digits with squishy curves, designed as a set (some coloured: sakura pink, yomogi green, white). Always alive at 60 fps: the rhythmic pounding (one pound each second, the other rabbit turning the dough between blows), squash and stretch, flour puffs drifting in low gravity. Minute turn: the old mochi digit is lifted into the mortar and pounded into a ball, then pulled and stretched into the new digit (a true physical transformation of the same dough, the time never wrong). Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the rabbits toss the hour mochi high in the low gravity and it lands as the new hour, or the Earth rises and lights everything. Rabbits must be bold and simple, 16+ px, with clear ears and eyes. Night: the moon side turns away from the sun, lit only by earthshine.
